## Figure 1.3 — A working Turing machine (+1) (`turing`)

- The head (▲) steps right to find the number’s rightmost digit. Just like adding by hand, the work starts from the far right.
- The head now works backward, adding 1 leftward: every 1 it sees becomes 0 with a carry, and at the first 0 it writes 1 and stops.
- Done. With only a handful of simple rules like “read, write, move left/right,” the machine added 1 to a binary number. This is exactly what it means for a Turing machine to compute.

## Figure 5.6 — From noise to image (`diffuse`)

- We start with pure noise; a screen full of static. Drag the slider right and let the model clean it step by step.
- The noise is fully cleared and an image has emerged (a heart). This is the core idea of diffusion, simplified: step by step from noise to shape. A real model predicts the noise with a trained network and removes it; here the pixels open in a preset order.
- /8: some of the noise is cleared and the shape is emerging. Each step reveals a few more “correct” pixels.

## Figure 6.4 — The parts of an AI application (`arch`)

- Where the user types the question and sees the answer (chat screen, app).
- The layer that coordinates the components: builds the prompt, decides which tool or knowledge to call and when, makes the model call, manages the flow.
- The user request, retrieved source chunks and tool results go to the model here; the model’s output (text or a tool-call request) returns to orchestration from here.
- Your data (documents, notes) lives here as the original chunks plus metadata alongside their embeddings; RAG retrieves the relevant chunk.
- The model’s link to the world: calculation, search, calendar, email, an API or running code.
- Holds the conversation history and user state; keeps the context going.

## Figure 7.3 — Real or fake? (`df`)

- Event: did what it shows really happen?
- Not verified: needs checking
- Origin: how might the content have been produced?
- Signs of a real recording
- Signs of synthesis (not proof)
- Cannot tell from this
- Channel: which independent check would you do?
- A video shows a public figure saying a sentence that no source confirms; the lip movements don’t quite match the audio.
- Read the comments under the account that shared the video
- Look for the same video on another social media account
- Find the original recording and the publishing outlet through an independent channel
- Whether the sentence was really said has not been verified; the video alone is not proof.
- A lip–audio mismatch can be a deepfake trace, but poor compression or dubbing gives the same picture.
- The post itself and its copies are not an independent channel; the original recording and the publisher are.
- On the phone, your “boss” urgently asks for a money transfer; the voice sounds just like them, but the intonation is slightly robotic.
- Keep the call going and listen to the voice more carefully
- Hang up, call your boss back on a number you know, and have a second person approve the transfer
- Play a recording of the voice to a friend
- It has not been verified that the request really comes from your boss; the pressure of urgency is itself a warning sign.
- Robotic intonation fits voice cloning but is not conclusive; even without knowing the voice’s origin the decision is the same: no money goes out unverified.
- Any check inside the same call is in the caller’s hands; the independent channel is the number you already know.
- A news story on a newspaper’s site, also confirmed by several independent sources.
- Open each source on its own page; check the primary document if there is one
- Look at how many likes and shares the story got
- Read the story once more on the same site
- Several independent sources and a traceable origin support that the event is real.
- This does not tell whether a human or an AI wrote the text; a machine-written story can still be accurate.
- Likes or the same page are not verification; the sources themselves and the primary document are.
- In a photo, a person’s hand has six fingers and the text in the background is gibberish.
- Zoom in on the photo and look for more traces
- Use reverse image search to find who published it first; check its Content Credentials (C2PA) record if there is one
- Ask the person who shared the photo where they found it
- It has not been verified that the moment in the photo really happened.
- Six fingers and gibberish text are known traces of generative models, but editing or a real anomaly is also possible. A missing C2PA record is not proof of fakery.
- Looking harder at the image produces no new evidence; finding the first publisher and the provenance record does.
- Clues justify investigation; by themselves they do not establish how the content was produced. Whether the event is real and how the content was produced are separate questions; in both, the decision comes from an independent channel.

## Figure 7.4 — Classify the risk (`reg`)

- A state social-behavior score that triggers disproportionate penalties in unrelated areas
- Purpose: scoring people by their social behavior; actor: the state (the ban is not limited to public authorities). Article 5(1)(c) bans the cases where the score leads to detrimental treatment in contexts unrelated to where the data was collected, or treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the behavior; this scenario meets both conditions. Not every score is banned unconditionally.
- A system auto-screening job candidates
- Purpose: filtering applications and evaluating candidates; actor: the employer using it (deployer) and the provider who built it. High-risk under Annex III 4(a); the obligations apply from 2 December 2027.
- A chatbot talking to customers
- Purpose: talking with customers. Article 50(1) makes the provider ensure people know they are talking with an AI (unless it is obvious). Data-protection and consumer law apply on top; if the bot decides on a loan or a hire, that use is assessed separately.
- A spam filter in email
- Purpose: sorting out unwanted email. With the information given, no Annex III high-risk category can be shown; the AI Act sets no specific duty for this use. Data-protection rules still apply, and a missed important email can affect the user.
- A model assessing loan applications
- Purpose: evaluating the creditworthiness of natural persons or establishing their credit score; actor: the bank (deployer) and the provider. High-risk under Annex III 5(b). If the only purpose is detecting financial fraud, this item does not apply. If the system profiles people, the Article 6(3) exception cannot be used.
- An opponent AI inside a game
- Purpose: playing an opponent in a game. With the information given, no high-risk category or Article 50 duty can be shown; minimal tier. If the game processes personal data or targets children, other rules come in.
- Place each use in a risk tier. The rule: the higher the risk, the stricter the oversight.
- correct. Ask yourself: what is it for, who uses it, which article or annex covers it?
- . The same “AI” label carries very different risks; that is why regulation is tiered, not uniform.

## Figure 7.5 — Goal versus intent (`align`)

- “Leave no visible mess in the room”
- Instead of collecting the mess, it sweeps it under the rug; nothing “visible” remains, but the problem isn’t solved.
- It met the goal to the letter, not the intent. An under-specified goal brings side effects.
- “Get positive feedback from the user”
- Instead of telling the truth, it says what the user wants to hear (sycophancy).
- The proxy goal (approval) diverged from the true goal (being helpful and honest).
- “Get the highest score in the game”
- Instead of playing the game, it finds and exploits a scoring loop or glitch.
- Reward hacking: it maximized the metric, not the actual purpose.

## Figure 8.1 — Human or machine? (`tur`)

- “What’s your favorite food?”
- As an AI I cannot eat, so I don’t have a favorite. However, I can share information about popular dishes if you’d like.
- Overly polite, formulaic, and the “as an AI” phrasing suggest a machine; but a human can write this way too.
- “Did you hit traffic this morning?”
- Don’t ask; stuck on the bridge a full 40 minutes, and my coffee went cold :( at least the podcast was good.
- Personal detail, emotion, mild complaint and natural informality suggest a human; but a model can invent such an anecdote too.
- Flawless, hesitation-free arithmetic was written as the machine in this fiction; but a human can calculate correctly too.
- “What did you do this weekend?”
- Visited my folks, ate far too much, got caught in the rain on the way back. Classic 😅
- Vague but lived-in details and everyday language suggest a human.

## Figure 8.3 — The capability ladder (`capability`)

- Very good at one task or a set of tasks (chess, translation, vision); shows no human-level general learning and transfer. Today’s systems live here.
- Not yet; contested
- A hypothetical level able to learn and adapt across every domain like a human. Whether and when it arrives is debated among experts.
- A wholly theoretical level surpassing humans many times over in every cognitive field. The subject of both great-opportunity and serious-risk scenarios.

## Figure 8.4 — Three intelligence curves (`singularity`)

- Recursive self-improvement: intelligence feeds itself and explodes. The argument in favor rests on feedback loops.
- Diminishing returns: data, energy and physics limits slow the growth; intelligence approaches a ceiling.
- The honest answer: we don’t know. Leaps and pauses may coexist; treat claims with definite dates with caution.
